status_reason: The target is defined, but the fluorescence concept is blocked for glucose, and the alternatives depend on the medium, concentration range and a viability reference, which are not yet given.
answer: Fluorescence should not be used to report glucose: it is very sensitive but not selective, and it has no direct route to glucose. Raman should be tested first for glucose, with NIR as the comparison method. Viable biomass needs its own defined reference before any inline signal can be trusted.

inline.headline: Test Raman for glucose in the fermentation broth against independent laboratory glucose values, with NIR as comparison
inline.probe: Raman fiber probe for liquids, excitation 785 nm (example laser in the lab set-up), spectral axis Raman shift in cm-1
inline.install: Inside the fermentation vessel at a port to be confirmed by the client
inline.fiber: Silica fiber in the Vis-NIR range (350-2400 nm), Al/Cu-coated to avoid polymer-jacket fluorescence
inline.test_against: NIR transmission or transflection probe for the same broth
inline.not_final_because: Raman signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence in many organic compounds; the sources give no glucose band positions or model, the medium and concentration range are unknown, and no viability reference exists.

problems.text: Sensitivity is not selectivity. Fluorescence gives a very strong signal, but most chemicals do not fluoresce, so a strong signal does not show that it comes from glucose.
Fluorescence has no direct route to glucose. Its intrinsic fluorophores are NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and a reference. Turbidity links to cell density and NIR with fluorescence improved yeast biomass, but no viable-cell measurement is described, so a viability reference is required.

methods.why: Gives direct detection of glucose and other metabolites and suits aqueous media because water absorbs weakly.
Tracks major components such as glucose in the millimolar range, but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 percent; it works with remote fiber probes.
Turbidity correlates with cell density and is a low-cost tool for biomass, but it is not a viability measure.
Detects only intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, so it cannot report glucose.

questions.why: The range decides whether NIR is sensitive enough or Raman is needed.

experiment.objective: Test whether Raman, with NIR as comparison, can follow glucose and biomass in real broth against independent laboratory references.
steps: Collect broth samples across the glucose and biomass range of one run and record the sample times.
Record Raman spectra (excitation 785 nm, Raman shift in cm-1) with an immersion probe and NIR spectra with a comparison probe, synchronised in time.
Measure glucose and viable cell count on the same samples by independent laboratory analysis, not by the instrument's own calibration.
Build one chemometric model per method on a calibration set and validate on held-out runs, comparing each against the best single method.
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria to be set by the client; accuracy and response time are not stated in the enquiry.

pathway.key_features: Glucose and biomass-related spectral features must be identified in the lab spectra; they are not given in the supplied claims.
pathway.path_reason: The AFS pathway requires a multi-method lab trial and key-feature selection before a model or system is chosen.

multispectral.why: NIR covers major components such as glucose at millimolar levels and Raman gives direct metabolite detection, so their information is complementary; the broth may not be heterogeneous, so separate synchronised probes are enough to start.
multispectral.test: Compare NIR + Raman against Raman alone on the same held-out samples; the combination counts only if it beats the best single method.
